# A Cluster-Randomised Trial of a 30-Hour Week in Municipal Administration: Nine-Month Results

*Varden County Evaluation Unit, in collaboration with the Department of Labour Economics, Easterly University. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony and D. Rao. Registered protocol VC-2023-04.*

## Summary

We randomly assigned 24 administrative offices of a county government, employing 1,180 staff, to either reduce scheduled hours from 37.5 to 30 per week at full pay (12 offices) or continue on the standard schedule (12 offices) for nine months. Output was measured from administrative records, not from manager assessments, and actual hours from timesheets. The effect differed sharply by type of work. In case-processing offices, where work arrives as a backlog that can be cleared at any time, output per full-time employee changed by −2.1% (95% CI −6.8 to +2.6) relative to control and output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. In counter and contact-centre offices, where output depends on staff being present while the public is waiting, output per employee fell by 11.4% (95% CI −16.9 to −5.9), waiting times rose, and output per actual hour rose by a more modest 6.7%. Sick days fell by 29% across treated offices. An exploratory analysis suggests that a reduction in recurring meetings may account for part of the gain in case-processing offices.

## Motivation

Existing evidence on reduced working time comes mainly from voluntary pilots without comparison groups, in which output is often reported by the managers who sponsored the change. The county wished to know whether a reduced schedule could be extended to its own administrative staff without loss of service, and agreed to a randomised design with administrative output measures and a registered analysis plan.

## Design

**Units and randomisation.** The 24 offices were stratified into two strata by type of work before randomisation, and offices were randomised within strata:

- *Case-processing offices* (14 offices; 7 treated, 7 control): permits, licensing, benefits assessment and records. Work arrives as cases that join a queue and can be completed at any point within statutory deadlines.
- *Counter and contact-centre offices* (10 offices; 5 treated, 5 control): in-person service counters and telephone lines. Work arrives as members of the public who must be served while they wait.

Randomisation was at office level to avoid contamination between colleagues. Treated offices kept their public opening hours unchanged; staff rotas were rearranged so that each employee worked 30 scheduled hours.

**Outcomes.** The registered primary outcome is output per full-time-equivalent employee (FTE), measured as cases closed (case-processing) or contacts handled (counter and contact centre), from the county's case-management and telephony systems. Registered secondary outcomes are output per actual hour (from timesheets, which include any overtime claimed), quality (the share of decisions overturned on appeal; for contact centres, the repeat-contact rate within seven days), average waiting time, and sick days. Analysis is difference-in-differences against the six-month pre-period, with standard errors clustered by office.

**Exploratory measures.** At the request of office managers we also collected calendar data on recurring meetings in month six. This was not part of the registered plan.

## Results

### Hours

Scheduled hours fell by 20% in treated offices. Actual hours, from timesheets, fell by less: by 13% in case-processing offices (from 37.9 to 33.0 per week) and by 17% in counter offices (from 37.6 to 31.2), the difference reflecting overtime claimed to clear backlogs in case-processing. Control offices' actual hours were stable.

### Output and quality

**Table 1. Difference-in-differences estimates at nine months, treated relative to control**

| Outcome | Case-processing (7 v 7 offices) | Counter and contact centre (5 v 5 offices) |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −11.4% (−16.9 to −5.9) |
| Actual hours per FTE | −13% | −17% |
| Output per actual hour | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +6.7% (+0.4 to +13.3) |
| Appeal overturn rate / repeat contact rate | 3.1% v 3.0% | 11.8% v 10.9% |
| Average wait (minutes), treated offices, pre → month 9 | — | 4.2 → 6.9 |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% (both strata pooled) | |

In case-processing offices, output per employee was statistically indistinguishable from control, with a point estimate slightly below zero, and quality was unchanged. Because actual hours fell by 13%, output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. Measured against scheduled rather than actual hours, the gain would appear as 22%; we regard that figure as misleading, because staff did not in fact work only the scheduled hours.

In counter and contact-centre offices, the picture is different. With the same number of staff each working fewer hours, fewer staff were present at any given time during unchanged opening hours. Contacts handled per employee fell by 11.4% and the average wait rose from 4.2 to 6.9 minutes. Output per actual hour rose by 6.7%, but this did not offset the loss of hours, and the service the public received was worse. Abandoned calls rose from 6% to 10% of calls.

### Wellbeing

Sick days fell by 29% in treated offices relative to control. Resignations were lower in treated offices (annualised 3.9% against 7.4%), though with 12 offices per arm and few resignations the estimate is imprecise.

### Exploratory: meetings

Calendar data in month six showed that staff in treated case-processing offices spent 3.8 hours per week in recurring meetings against 7.1 hours in control case-processing offices, a difference of 3.3 hours. Offices that cut meetings most showed the largest gains in output per hour (correlation across the 7 treated offices, r = 0.71). Interviews suggested that the reduced schedule prompted managers to cancel standing meetings that had persisted by habit.

We emphasise that this analysis was not registered, that it rests on seven offices, and that a correlation across seven offices cannot establish a mechanism. We report it because, if confirmed, it would mean that a substantial part of the per-hour gain comes from removing low-value time rather than from rest alone, and that would matter for how the result is interpreted and for what other employers could expect. We have registered a confirmatory test for the 24-month follow-up.

## Discussion

Three conclusions follow from the registered analyses.

First, in work where output is not tied to presence, a 20% cut in scheduled hours produced a much smaller cut in actual hours and little or no measurable loss of output per employee. Output per hour rose by about an eighth.

Second, in work where output is tied to presence, the same change reduced output per employee by about a tenth and worsened service, even though each hour worked was somewhat more productive. Gains per hour do not by themselves imply that the hours reduction pays for itself. The question "does a shorter week raise productivity?" therefore has at least two answers depending on whether productivity is understood per hour or per employee, and these come apart most sharply in coverage-bound work.

Third, estimates computed against scheduled hours materially overstate the per-hour gain. In our data the overstatement is from 12.5% to 22% in case-processing offices.

These findings qualify claims, made on the basis of uncontrolled pilots, that reduced hours are sector-general. A sector may contain both kinds of work; what matters is whether output in a given role depends on hours of presence.

## Limitations

The trial is in one public employer, with 24 offices; confidence intervals are correspondingly wide, particularly in the counter stratum. Staff knew their assignment, and control staff knew that a trial was under way, which could have affected effort in either direction. Nine months may be too short to reveal whether gains persist after the novelty of the change wears off, or whether backlogs build up beyond the statutory deadlines. Public-sector case processing may differ from private-sector knowledge work in ways that affect the result. A 24-month follow-up is under way.

response:
# Review: "A Cluster-Randomised Trial of a 30-Hour Week in Municipal Administration"

This is a much stronger study than the Halden pilot. It addresses most of that paper's main weaknesses:

- **Design:** offices were randomised, with stratification by type of work.
- **Outcomes:** output comes from administrative records, and actual hours come from timesheets.
- **Analysis:** there is a registered plan, CIs are reported, and exploratory work is clearly labelled.
- **Interpretation:** the authors explicitly reject the per-scheduled-hour figure.

The arithmetic checks out:
- Case-processing hours fell 12.9%, and 0.979/0.87 gives +12.5% per actual hour (+22.4% against scheduled hours).
- Counter hours fell 17.0%, and 0.886/0.83 gives +6.7% per actual hour.
- "About an eighth" and "about a tenth" are accurate.

The problems are subtler than in the Halden paper. Several of them affect the headline conclusions.

## 1. Cost is missing, and overtime makes it central

Case-processing staff worked 33.0 actual hours against 30 scheduled, so about 3 hours a week of overtime, compared with about 0.4 before. The paper says this reflects "overtime claimed." If that overtime was paid, possibly at a premium, on top of unchanged base pay:

- Labour cost per FTE may have risen by roughly 10–15%, depending on the premium.
- Output per FTE was flat or slightly down (−2.1%).
- So **cost per case may have risen materially**, even in the stratum the paper presents as the success.

The county's stated question was whether the schedule could be extended "without loss of service." For a public employer, cost is part of that question.

Please report:
- whether overtime was paid or taken as time off in lieu, and at what rate;
- total labour cost per unit of output, by stratum.

It also matters whether the overtime is transitional (clearing a backlog) or structural. In other words, is the case-processing result sustained partly by working longer than 30 hours?

## 2. The per-hour gain in counter offices is probably queueing, not productivity

The paper reads the +6.7% as each hour being "somewhat more productive." In demand-driven work, a mechanical explanation is more likely.

- With fewer staff present during the same opening hours, queues lengthen.
- Longer queues mean each staff member spends less time idle between contacts.
- Contacts per hour therefore rise because of higher utilisation, even if nobody works faster.
- The cost of that higher utilisation is borne by the public as waiting time, which rose from 4.2 to 6.9 minutes.

This changes the interpretation of the Discussion's second conclusion. A queueing explanation predicts exactly this pattern without any change in effort or fatigue. The authors could test it with occupancy or idle-time data from the telephony system. If utilisation rose by roughly 6–7%, there is nothing left for a rest-based explanation to account for.

There is a smaller related issue. Repeat contacts are counted as output, and the repeat-contact rate was higher in treated offices (11.8% against 10.9%). Part of the measured output is therefore rework.

## 3. The counter-stratum numbers need reconciling, and demand may have spilled over

The paper reports two figures that don't obviously fit together:
- Abandoned calls rose from 6% to 10%. If demand was constant, handled calls would fall by only about 4% (from 94% to 90% of demand).
- Yet contacts handled per employee fell by 11.4%.

Possible explanations include:
- demand at treated offices fell, for example because people stopped attending counters with long waits;
- the abandonment figure covers telephone only, while the 11.4% covers both counters and phones;
- **demand moved from treated offices to control offices.**

The third possibility is a real threat to the design. Randomising at office level prevents contamination between colleagues. It does not stop the public going to a different counter, or telephone overflow being routed to another centre.

If displaced demand raised control offices' output, the difference-in-differences estimate overstates the loss in two ways:
- it counts work that was redistributed rather than lost;
- it may inflate control offices' workload.

The same question applies to case processing if cases can be reassigned between offices. The paper should report demand at each office and say how overflow is routed.

## 4. Inference with very few clusters

There are only 10 clusters in the counter stratum (5 against 5) and 14 in case processing. Conventional cluster-robust standard errors are known to be too small with this few clusters, so the counter CI (−16.9 to −5.9) is likely too narrow.

Use one of the following:
- wild cluster bootstrap;
- randomisation inference, which is natural here because the stratified assignment is known;
- small-sample-corrected standard errors (CR2 with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom).

The counter output effect is large enough that it will probably survive this correction. The counter per-hour CI (+0.4 to +13.3) probably will not.

## 5. Sick days may fall mechanically

The paper doesn't say how rotas were rearranged. If staff moved to four days a week, each employee has 20% fewer working days on which to be absent. Sick days per FTE would then fall about 20% even if the underlying rate of illness was unchanged. Against that benchmark, the reported −29% is much less striking.

Report sickness per scheduled day, or as hours lost as a share of scheduled hours. Also report the schedule structure, meaning fewer days versus shorter days, by office. The same caveat applies to the Halden pilot's −36%.

## 6. Results not reported as the registered design requires

Several outcomes are not reported as difference-in-differences estimates with CIs, even though the registered analysis is DiD:

| Outcome | As reported | Problem |
|---|---|---|
| Quality (overturn / repeat-contact rate) | Levels only, treated v control | No DiD, no CI. The counter difference (+0.9 pp, about 8% relative) goes unremarked, while case-processing quality is called "unchanged." |
| Average wait | Treated pre → month 9 only | No control comparison. Seasonal or system-wide changes cannot be excluded. |
| Abandoned calls | Text only | Not registered, no control comparison. |
| Resignations | Raw annualised rates | Not registered, no DiD, no CI. It is correctly called imprecise, but should be labelled exploratory. |

**Quality data are censored.** Appeals take time to be lodged and decided, so decisions made in months 7–9 mostly cannot yet have been overturned. "Quality unchanged" is therefore premature for the later part of the trial. Restrict the measure to decisions old enough to have passed the appeal window, or report it with that caveat.

**Backlog size is available now.** The Limitations section mentions that backlogs might build up. The case-management system should already record queue length, case age and compliance with statutory deadlines. These are direct tests of whether case-processing output is being sustained or deferred.

## 7. The meetings analysis may understate its own implication

The authors are appropriately cautious. The analysis is unregistered, based on seven offices, and a confirmatory test is registered. The confidence interval for r = 0.71 with n = 7 runs from roughly 0 to 0.95.

A rough back-of-envelope calculation suggests the point matters more than "part of the gain." It assumes treated offices' pre-trial meeting time was similar to control offices' 7.1 hours, which randomisation makes plausible but which wasn't measured. On that assumption:

- Hours not spent in meetings fell from about 30.8 to 29.2, roughly −5%.
- Output changed by about −2%.
- Output per non-meeting hour therefore rose by only about 3%.

If meeting time produced little output, meeting cuts could account for **most** of the 12.5%, not part of it. That bears directly on the policy question: an employer might get much of the gain by cutting meetings without cutting hours. It could also be stated in the confirmatory plan.

Two further points:
- The "interviews" are not described in the Methods section.
- Meeting data were collected at managers' request, and treated managers had a stake in the result.

## 8. Smaller points

- **Wording:** the Summary says sick days fell 29% "across treated offices." It should say "relative to control."
- **FTE definition:** confirm that "per FTE" means per employee on the original 37.5-hour basis, and that headcount was unchanged in both arms. The text says "same number of staff" only for counter offices.
- **Pre-specified subgroups:** state whether stratum-specific primary effects were pre-specified. Stratification suggests they were, but it is worth saying explicitly.
- **Scope of the counter result:** the counter finding depends on how the trial was implemented, with fixed headcount and unchanged opening hours. The Discussion should say that this tests one way of implementing reduced hours in coverage-bound work, not every way. Hiring or changing opening hours would trade the service loss for cost.
- **Control-arm resentment:** the Limitations section notes awareness effects. Resentment could depress control output, which would bias the DiD in treated offices' favour. That direction is worth stating specifically.

## Overall

The main conclusions are well supported:
- the effect of reduced hours depends on whether output is tied to presence;
- per-scheduled-hour figures overstate gains;
- uncontrolled pilots' claims of sector-generality don't hold up.

The most important additions are:
1. cost per unit of output, including overtime;
2. a test of whether the counter per-hour gain is just higher utilisation;
3. checks for demand spillover to control offices;
4. small-cluster inference;
5. sickness adjusted for schedule structure.

The first two could change how readers interpret the case-processing "success" and the counter "per-hour gain."

I can draft a revised Results table showing the missing DiD estimates, or a short note setting out the queueing and meetings arithmetic, if either would help.
